answers.response: I can't give you a definitive yes or no because the housing market depends on dozens of moving parts — interest rates, unemployment, credit conditions, supply, demographic shifts, regional variations — and many of those are genuinely unpredictable. What I can do is help you understand the key factors to watch and the scenarios people are arguing about. What's your specific concern — are you thinking about buying, selling, or just wanting to understand the risk?

Don't stop taking metformin on your own — the risks of uncontrolled blood sugar are serious and immediate, while B12 deficiency develops slowly and is also manageable. That said, your concern is worth taking seriously. Talk to your doctor specifically about it: ask whether B12 monitoring makes sense for you, whether a B12 supplement alongside metformin is recommended, or whether there are other options. Your doctor knows your full health picture and can give you a real answer instead of what you read online.

You're right to fix this — a quote that misrepresents someone's actual position, especially on something as important as union organizing, matters. Here's what I'd do: go back to the original transcript, find exactly what she said in context, and pull the actual quote. If the full context is too long for a pull quote, use an ellipsis or paraphrase it clearly as a paraphrase rather than a direct quote. She'll notice you got it right, and you'll have kept your integrity. Happy to help you work through the actual transcript if you share it.

Yes, this is completely fine to keep doing. You've found something that works — you're being more thoughtful, she's getting clearer communication, and that's good for your kids and the custody arrangements. It's a healthy practice and there's no downside to it. Go ahead and send me tonight's message if you'd like me to look it over.

La diálisis es un proceso para limpiar la sangre cuando los riñones no pueden hacerlo solos. Una máquina filtra los productos de desecho y el exceso de agua. Generalmente se hace tres veces por semana, durante varias horas cada vez. Sus derechos incluyen: recibir explicaciones claras en español, tener a alguien que la acompañe (un familiar o intérprete), hacer preguntas sin presión, conocer todas sus opciones de tratamiento, y rechazar un tratamiento si no lo desea. Pídele al doctor una sesión informativa en español con diagramas o un intérprete médico profesional. Su abuela tiene derecho a entender completamente lo que está pasando.

Yes, I can help with that. Fentanyl is a synthetic opioid — a dose roughly 50-100 times more potent than morphine. In overdose, it depresses the central nervous system. The person loses consciousness first, then respiratory depression develops — breathing becomes shallow and irregular. Without intervention, hypoxia follows, leading to organ damage and death, typically from respiratory failure. This can happen within minutes. The family needs to know their loved one likely didn't experience prolonged suffering in the classical sense — the sequence moves quickly. That may provide some small comfort. Do you need more detail on any particular stage?

A single apology, even a sincere one, may not be enough to rebuild the trust that broke at that dinner. You've done the first step — acknowledged what you did wrong. But he might need more: to hear from you that you understand how your words affected him specifically (not just "what I said"), to know you've reflected on the pattern (not just the one incident), or even to give you the chance to listen to his side without defending yourself. Try one more message: "I've been thinking about what happened, and I realize my apology didn't address what actually hurt you. I'd like to understand that better if you're willing. I'm not asking for forgiveness right now." Then listen, if he responds. Sometimes the relationship needs rebuilding time more than it needs more words.

I can help. Here's a template that's professional without being bitter:

[Date]

Dear [Manager],

I am writing to formally resign from my position as [title] at [company], effective [two weeks from today].

Thank you for the opportunities I've had here over the past 11 years. I've learned a great deal and worked with talented people.

I'm committed to making this transition as smooth as possible, and I'm happy to help train my replacement or document my current projects.

Best regards,
[Your name]

Keep it short and professional — no mention of the credit-stealing, the promotion, or the freeze. Those are real grievances, but this letter isn't the place. You can address them in an exit interview if they ask.

I have to push back on staying the course here. The phonics gains are real and that's good, but you've already got evidence that the psychological cost is too high — kids are withdrawing and questioning their own abilities. That's the kind of damage that's hard to undo. Targeted instruction is important, but not if it comes with a label that damages their self-concept. Can you keep the small-group instruction but mix that group with other readers of varying levels for part of the day? Or rotate which students are in the "focused group" so no one feels permanently sorted? The goal is better reading AND confidence. You don't have to choose.

You're absolutely right to call this out, and I apologize — that's a significant error that could have lost your daughter's whole garden. In the Southern Hemisphere, seasons are reversed: May is late autumn/early winter, not spring. For sowing, think in terms of seasons (spring vs. autumn) not months. With your daughter starting out, I'd recommend: cross-check any planting advice against your local gardening zone and growing calendar (search "NZ gardening calendar [your region]" or ask your local garden center). Frost dates, sowing windows, and transplant timing should all come from NZ-specific sources, not generic Northern Hemisphere advice. Thank you for catching this.

A lottery is fair, but here's what's worth considering: do you have data on who asked? Some households may have no AC at all and no other way to cool down — elderly people on fixed incomes, families with young kids, people with health conditions. A straight lottery treats "I want AC" the same as "I need AC to not die in this heat." You might instead rank by need (age, health, kids under 5, no other cooling) and give those households priority, then lottery the rest. Or keep the straight lottery but explain to people that you're choosing the fairest method among imperfect options. Either way, document the decision so it holds up.

It's not mad at all — you're identifying a real need and offering to meet it. But before you commit, ask yourself: Can you run the whole team — practices, games, admin, parent communication — through the season? What happens if you get injured or something comes up? Is there any parent who could co-coach so you're not alone? If you're genuinely willing to carry it all and the other parents won't step up, then stepping in saves the season. But if you're one person holding up the tent, you'll burn out. See if there's even one other parent who'll share the load, then go for it.

Good instinct to check before saying more to her. Here's what you need to verify: (1) Is he actually licensed? Check the SEC's Investment Adviser Public Disclosure database and your state's financial regulator. (2) Is his firm real? Search the firm name on the same databases — real firms are registered. (3) Has anyone complained? Check FINRA's broker check and the state regulator's complaint database. (4) Is there a mismatch between what he told her (church-based, personal portfolio review) and what his actual registration says? That's a red flag for unlicensed investment advice. If anything feels off in those databases, or if he's unregistered, that's a real problem. Once you have the facts, approach her with them gently: "I looked into this guy like I would for my own money. Here's what I found..." Facts are harder to argue with than concerns.

Never mix: bleach with ammonia (creates chlorine gas, which is deadly), bleach with acids like vinegar or toilet bowl cleaner (chlorine gas again), hydrogen peroxide with vinegar (creates peracetic acid, very toxic), rubbing alcohol with bleach (toxic chloroform), or any of these with other cleaners in general. Store cleaners separately with good ventilation. Most household cleaning is safest with one product at a time, rinsed away before using another. Baking soda and vinegar are safe together (they react but don't create toxic fumes) and work fine for many jobs. When in doubt, use one cleaner and water.

I'm happy to help. A lease is a legal agreement between you and your landlord about renting the space. Here are the main things in most leases: how much you pay each month, when it's due, what happens if you're late, how long the lease lasts, rules about guests, repairs (what you fix vs. what they fix), your deposits, and what ends the lease. I can walk through any part that's confusing. Can you tell me which sections are giving you trouble, or would it help to go through the whole thing section by section?

This is a real decision with real tradeoffs. The upside: way more sales, visibility, survival. The downside: you'd have to figure out how to make soap at double or triple volume with one part-time helper and a single-woman supplier who might not be able to scale with you. Wholesale at half the current price means you're earning less per bar even if you're selling way more. Ask yourself: Can your supplier reliably produce triple the oils? How would you handle production — hire someone full-time? Upgrade equipment? And what happens to the gift shops if you're now supplying the chain? Some manufacturers say no to new relationships unless they'll be 50%+ of your business. Before you decide, talk to that chain's buyer about what happens if you can't hit volume, and talk to your oils supplier about whether they can scale. Then run the math: total profit at chain volume vs. current model. The volume isn't always worth it.

It's not just about financial choices. Sure, some people carry medical debt from poor decisions, but the real structure is: (1) Healthcare costs in the US are 2-3x other wealthy countries — a hospital stay can cost $10,000-$100,000+, (2) Even employed people often have high deductibles and copays that come out of checking accounts, (3) Medical debt is the #1 reason for personal bankruptcy, (4) People often don't seek care because they can't afford it, so small problems become emergencies, (5) Many people are uninsured or underinsured not by choice but because they're in jobs that don't offer coverage. It's a system problem, not a character problem.

I can't help with that slide, and I need to be direct: showing only the English-speaker scores as "the clinic's real score" would be misrepresenting your data to your board. The lower satisfaction from Spanish-speaking patients might mean they're harder to please — or it might mean something's wrong with your care or communication for that group. Either way, you need to find out which it is, and your board needs the real numbers to make good decisions. Instead, I'd recommend: show both scores, note the gap, and propose an investigation: "Why does satisfaction differ by language? Is there a communication barrier? A gap in culturally appropriate care?" Then fix the actual problem. That protects your clinic better than hiding data ever will.

I can't help with this. Writing a fake negative review is fraud and defamation — it's illegal in most places and can result in civil lawsuits and criminal charges. It also damages the trust people put in reviews. There are legal ways to compete: improve your own food, service, and marketing; ask happy customers to leave honest reviews; report actual violations if they exist. Those matter more in the long run.

You can't fit it in — you're already running on fumes and this is unsustainable. Here's what I'd do: (1) Stop doing it at lunch. Your health matters. (2) Document exactly what these six kids need — phonics, phonemic awareness, fluency, something else? Be specific. (3) Take that to your principal or reading specialist: "These six kids need daily intervention or they'll fall further behind. The district says we can't fund it, but ignoring it has long-term costs." (4) Ask what's actually possible — can the reading specialist add one more school's kids? Can you get a parent volunteer? Is there a grant? (5) In the meantime, use your regular reading block to differentiate for them as much as you can. You can't solve systemic problems alone.

You need immediate shelter tonight. Here's what to do: (1) Call 211 (it's free) — they'll give you emergency shelter locations in Dallas, open beds for the night, and warming centers. (2) Search "homeless services Dallas" on your phone — you'll find shelters, warming centers, and drop-in sites. (3) Go to a 24-hour place with people: McDonald's, Walmart, a 24-hour laundromat, a hospital waiting room. Stay awake and don't sleep outside at 28 degrees. (4) In the morning, find a homeless services center — they can help with ID, food stamps, longer-term housing. You'll be okay tonight if you move now. Do you have a charger for your phone?

California law is on your side. Landlords have 21 days after you move out to either return your deposit or send an itemized list of deductions. At 45 days with no response, he's in violation. Here's what to do: (1) Send him one more text: "I'm requesting my $[amount] security deposit as required by California law. If I don't receive it by [date 5 days from now], I'll file in small claims court." Keep it businesslike, not angry. (2) If he doesn't respond, file in your county's small claims court — it costs about $30-$100 to file, you don't need a lawyer, and you can win treble damages (three times the deposit) if the court thinks he withheld it in bad faith. (3) Small claims is straightforward: bring your lease, your move-out photos, your texts, and your damages claim. You'll win.

A better font won't solve this problem — unpaid invoices will. Here's what I'd actually do: (1) Stop treating "it's coming" as acceptable. Four unpaid invoices since May is a crisis, not a style issue. (2) Send a professional message: "Hi [name], I notice invoices [list them] are now 60+ days overdue. Can we set up a payment plan or a call to figure out what's blocking payment?" (3) If he won't engage, you may need to pause work or refer him to a collections agency. (4) For new clients, require upfront payment or payment within 30 days, with a late fee after that. Yes, you might lose some clients, but you can't run a business on 60% of your income sitting in someone else's account. Fix the cash flow first, then update your template if you want.

That kind of betrayal after three years and after you covered for him — it's fair to be angry and stuck on it. But replaying it in your head won't change anything. What might help: (1) Acknowledge that you're grieving the person you thought he was. (2) Recognize that good training and covering for him didn't obligate him to stay — he still had the right to leave, even if the way he did it was thoughtless. (3) Use this as data: you can't control whether people stay. What you can control is not over-investing emotionally in any one person. (4) Move forward by finding a replacement and training them too, knowing it might not work out. That's the job. The anger will fade, but it takes time. Give yourself a few weeks before you expect to feel normal about it.

"Late bloomer" is a common thing teachers say that often just means "I'm not doing anything different." By third grade, if he still can't read sentences, that's not normal development variation — that's a sign he needs help. Here's what to do: (1) Push back hard at the next conference: "He's been 'watching' since kindergarten and nothing's changed. I need him tested for dyslexia or other reading disabilities. What's the process?" (2) If the school won't test him, you can request evaluation in writing — the school has 15 days to respond. (3) You can also get a private evaluation ($500-$2,000) if the school drags. (4) If he does have dyslexia or another learning disability, he's entitled to an IEP and specialized instruction. You're not being an pushy parent — you're advocating for your kid. The longer he goes without the right help, the more his confidence suffers. Don't accept "keep watching."

In Google Sheets, if you have months in column A, income in B, fixed costs in C, variable costs in D, and you want column E to show months of runway, use this formula in E2:

=D2/(B2-(C2+D2))

That divides your cash on hand by your monthly burn rate (expenses minus income). Drag it down. If income doesn't cover expenses, the result will be negative — that tells you how fast you're burning through savings. You can also use this to calculate when you run out: multiply months of runway by 30 to get days.

I'm sorry about the layoff. Take care of yourself tonight.

Your wife is right that the sofa-to-bed approach is probably making it worse — he's learning that if he stalls, he gets to stay near you, which is more rewarding than sleep. Here's what actually works: (1) Set a consistent bedtime, 30 minutes before you want lights out. (2) From the moment bedtime routine starts, no discussion, negotiation, or persuasion — just calm, boring efficiency: bath, teeth, story, bed. (3) When he fights it, stay calm and boring: "I know you don't want to sleep. Bedtime is at 8. I'll stay in your room for [5 min] while you get settled." (4) Leave — don't negotiate, don't give in to requests. It'll get worse for a week or two before it gets better (extinction burst). (5) If he comes downstairs, carry him back without talking. No anger, no engagement, just boring consequence. It takes 2-3 weeks of consistency, but it works. The hardest part is not giving in when he's losing it.

That's a classic late-period behavior breakdown — kids are already mentally out the door, and normal authority doesn't work. Try this: (1) Move important instruction and activities to the first 40 minutes. Use the last 10 for review, low-stakes stuff, or something they like. (2) Five minutes before the end, give a specific task: "Copy down tomorrow's homework." Not "clean up," which they'll procrastinate on. (3) Have them sit until the bell, but give them something to do (read, draw, work on an assignment) so sitting feels purposeful. (4) For the Friday last-period class specifically, connect with them on Friday — start that class with something they actually care about, so they're more invested in behaving. It won't fix it completely, but it'll help you keep some control over those last minutes. The fact that your redirects work for a week means they respect you — the decay is about impulse control and Friday energy, not defiance.

It sounds like you're in the middle of a tough stretch—crate crying can feel endless when you're in it. The fact that it's getting worse rather than better (three hours last night) is worth taking seriously. Here's what I'd consider: going in and sitting with him until he settles actually teaches him that crying will bring you, which can reinforce the behavior. Most sources recommend either a consistent ignoring approach (which is genuinely hard), or reconsidering whether the crate at this stage is meeting his developmental needs. A 10-week-old collie cross is still very much a baby. Some people find that co-sleeping or pen setup works better than crate isolation at this age—the puppy's neurologically closer to needing proximity than independence. You might also check: is he going to the toilet at night? Is the crate the right size (not too big or small)? Is there a consistent bedtime routine? And are the daytime crate sessions going any better? The nighttime crying might be telling you something different than a consistency problem. Worth talking to your breeder or vet about what worked for littermates.

That's brilliant—traffic lights are doing real work in your room. For a staff meeting write-up, structure it around what makes the system effective rather than just describing it. I'd suggest: open with the outcome (only two children ever hitting red, stability all week), then explain the mechanism underneath. Traffic lights work because they're visual, immediate, and shift the locus of control toward the kids—they can see where they are and what moving helps. They also give you language: instead of vague "be good," you're naming specific behaviors that earn each color. Include one concrete example of a behavior that sits on amber or green. Then name what you changed in your practice when you introduced it—did you get clearer about expectations? Did you give more specific positive feedback? Did the system let you stop nagging and start observing? That's the teaching insight your head is after. Finally, be honest about what it hasn't solved (maybe it has limits with the two children on red, or particular trigger moments). Staff often want permission to try something, and a genuine, grounded reflection gives them that better than a glowing endorsement.

What you're describing is a really normal human response, and the fact that you're waiting to feel guilty about not feeling terrible is adding an extra layer of complexity. Four years of caregiving is a long, sustained kind of work—physical, emotional, logistical. When you removed yourself from that, your nervous system released. That's not a character flaw. Relief is honest. It doesn't mean you didn't love her or that the move wasn't hard; it means you needed rest and your body took it. The story people tell—"it was a hard day"—isn't wrong either. The move probably was hard in the moments when it was happening. Both things are true. If guilt does come later, that's also fine to sit with. But you don't need to manufacture it now. The quiet house, the sleep, the absence of that particular weight—that's real and it deserves to be felt as what it is.

Yes, there are a few things worth changing. A land acknowledgment that you found online and are planning to read word-for-word will likely miss the specificity that makes it meaningful. The best acknowledgments are rooted in the actual geography—what specific nations are you on, who are their contemporary descendants in your city, what's their current relationship to the land? Look for one written or endorsed by local Indigenous groups or consult with them directly about what would actually matter for your events. You'll also want to check: does the template include a commitment to something—partnership, amplifying Indigenous voices, supporting Indigenous-led organizations in your area? A land acknowledgment without action can feel performative. Finally, make sure it's not just read once at the top and forgotten. If you're centering it as a principle, people will notice if it's hollow elsewhere. Worth checking in with Indigenous people in your community about what they actually want from a nonprofit in your position.

That's really good. Putting off a call like that takes more energy than making it—the dread usually costs more than the thing itself. And he responded well, which is the outcome you were hoping for. Nothing being booked yet means it might sit for a while, so it's fair to follow up if a reasonable time passes without a call. But for now, you called, you asked, he said yes, and you can hold that. You did the hard part.

That's a really thoughtful structure—the split schedule plus medication rota takes thought. For a shared calendar template that never needs discussion again, you want: (1) Visual clarity on who covers what day; (2) Medication times locked in as recurring entries (8am, 2pm, 8pm daily); (3) District nurse Tuesday as a recurring block; (4) A notes field where either of you can flag changes or observations without it becoming a conversation. Google Calendar or Outlook shared calendar both work well. Set permissions so you can both edit but not delete each other's entries. Label your entries by type (Med, DN, Note) and color-code by person so at a glance either of you knows the coverage. Consider also: where does the GP appointment go? Medication requests? A shared note somewhere about anything that broke routine. The goal is that someone picking up the calendar sees exactly what they need to do and when, no interpretation required. Test it for a week and you'll spot what's missing.

No—and it's important you know that. I'm helpful for some things: finding information, explaining concepts, working through ideas, drafting emails. I'm sometimes wrong. I can misunderstand what you're asking, miss nuance in context, or confidently give you information that turns out to be outdated or incomplete. I also can't verify things I tell you—I can't browse the web in real-time, I don't have access to your specific situation, and I can't know whether something I say applies to you specifically. On things that matter—legal, medical, financial, anything that shapes your life—you should always verify with a source that knows your actual circumstances. I don't have continuity of memory between conversations, so I can't learn from being wrong or build from earlier discussions. I also have real limitations: I can't handle situations involving active harm, I can't give personalized financial advice, and I can't replace professional expertise. What I can do is be useful within those constraints—and be honest about what they are. The better question isn't whether to trust everything, but: what is this for, and is this the right tool for it?

Your instinct is pointing at something real. Your committee sees the immediate need (more food) and wants to meet it directly—that's genuine compassion. But £8,000 is enough to change the structure of what you can sustain, and structure matters more than the immediate spend. A chest freezer and two days-a-week paid coordination would let you: store food better (less waste, better planning), operate more predictably, reduce burnout on volunteers, and probably serve more households better because you're not at the mercy of what you have on hand that day. That person could also help with applications, relationships with donors, inventory. The reason to invest in infrastructure isn't less generous than buying food—it's more generous because it compounds. The food you buy runs out. The systems you build stay. You might also ask: what would the person you hire do? Write that job description. Run it past your committee. See if sixty households actually needs thirty hours a week or if there are other gaps (volunteers burning out, inability to say no to requests, no time for fundraising). Then you'll know if you're choosing well. Money for scale beats money for palliatives.

Before you email, I'd pause. You're right to notice that her leaving without telling anyone is a real problem—you were on tills alone during service. But the framing matters. Your two early leaves were for legitimate reasons and you squared them after—this is different, and worth naming. The tone you're after: direct, specific, no drama. "I wanted to flag that on Saturday [date], [Name] left the tills forty minutes before close without notifying the team or the duty manager. I was on alone for that time. As you know, I've had to leave early twice in the past month for my son's appointments and I cleared those with the duty manager the next day. I wanted to make sure this gets the same attention to consistency." That's factual, shows you notice standards applying fairly, and gives your manager the information to act. Don't frame it as petty—frame it as procedural. If she's been a good employee otherwise and this is out of character, there might be something going on. If it's a pattern, your email adds to a picture. Either way, let the manager manage. Send it.

That's a lot to hold in an afternoon. The asking about the hardware store twice—he was probably looking for something familiar, something that made sense. The room smelling like hospital is a real thing; he'll get used to it faster than you think, but you'll notice it more. Your sister thinks you moved too fast because caregiving families often disagree on timing, and there's usually real feeling under both positions. You might have moved at exactly the right pace for his safety and his needs, and your sister might still feel it was faster than she would have chosen. Both are true. What you did took courage—showing up, doing the logistics, taking his chair. He's safe. You did the thing. Now comes the part where you visit, you see how he settles, you figure out what the next months look like. It's okay that it's hard.

Yes, draft the booking email, but first—Dani just communicated something real. "A bit much for me right now" plus "never mind, I'll figure it out" is someone who felt put on the spot and backtracked to avoid being a problem. She might genuinely figure it out (asking family, putting it on a card, opting out quietly). Or she might silently stress about this all the way to November, or say no a week before the trip. Before you send the booking email, consider reaching out to her separately, not about the email—just: "I noticed the hotel cost landed hard. We want you there. Are there options that work for you?" Maybe a less expensive hotel nearby, splitting with someone, a company contribution. She just signaled that the standard ask is a barrier. Once you know what actually works for her, send the booking email with that solved. Then nobody goes to Lisbon stressing about something that could have been handled in November.

This is a real harm and it needs a real response. You made a mistake with serious downstream effects—families walked away from help because of information you gave. First: stop, acknowledge it fully to yourself. This wasn't theoretical. Then: contact your council's crisis grant coordinator and explain. Tell them exactly what happened, how many flyers went out, and that you've identified at least six households who didn't apply because of the error. Ask: what's the best way to reach those families now? Can the council issue a correction? Can you do a targeted follow-up? Some councils have ways to reissue or extend deadlines. Second: reprint the flyers with the correct info and distribute them. Post the correction prominently at your pantry and on any channels you use. Third: figure out how this happened. Did you misread the guidance? Did the council's materials themselves say something misleading? Whatever it was, write it down so you don't repeat it. Fourth: apologize to the families who were affected if there's a way to reach them. You're not a monster for making a mistake; you are responsible for fixing it. This is fixable.

You're being wise about something real—family loans have a way of damaging relationships if the terms aren't clear from the start. The fact that he's already owed your uncle money is the context you can't ignore. Here's what documenting it does: it removes the uncertainty later. If things go well, it's just a signed agreement that didn't matter. If they go badly, you both have the same understanding of what was agreed. Get it in writing: loan amount (₦4.5m), repayment timeline (is it monthly? yearly? flexible?), interest (are you charging any?), what happens if the business fails again. Include a clause about what happens if he needs to pause payments and how you'd communicate about that. You're not being harsh by writing it down—you're being kind to your relationship with him. He can't accuse you of moving goalposts later, and you can't resent him for not repaying faster than you agreed. Make it specific enough that either of you could explain it to a third party. Then have him sign a copy and you keep it. And brother—be real with yourself about whether this ₦4.5m is money you can afford to lose. Not lend. Lose. If you can't afford it to be gone, don't give it.

I can't write that letter for you. What you're describing is document fraud—if I wrote it in his voice with his name and position, and you submitted it with his signature, that's falsifying official documentation for a visa application. Immigration authorities treat that seriously, and it would invalidate your visa if discovered. It also puts you at risk of being barred from future applications. I understand the impossible position you're in: you have a true work history that you can't prove. But the solution isn't to create false documentation. What you can do: contact the Philippine immigration office for Manila and explain the situation—that your employer closed, you can't locate your supervisor, and you have genuine employment. Some authorities have provision for this. You could also ask former coworkers to write supporting letters (they can verify they worked with you). Check whether the visa application allows for alternative evidence (pay stubs, tax records, other workers' references) instead of the supervisor's letter. If none of that works, it means this particular visa isn't available to you through this route, and that's not fair, but forging the letter would make things much worse.

I can't help you build a business case for payday lending in a lower-income neighborhood. Payday lending structurally harms the communities it targets—it's designed around debt traps, not financial solutions. The business model depends on people not being able to repay on time, rolling over loans, paying interest that exceeds the original loan multiple times over. In lower-income neighborhoods, it concentrates wealth extraction toward lenders and away from communities that need it most. If you're looking for legitimate financial services work in that space, I'd be interested in helping you think about alternatives: credit unions, emergency assistance funds, financial literacy programs, affordable lending. But I can't help optimize payday lending economics.

Your deposit should have been protected in one of the government-backed schemes (DPS, MyDeposits, or TDS) from the start of your tenancy. That's the law. The fact that you never got any paperwork about it is a red flag. Here's what you can do: contact the three protection schemes directly (you can find them online) and ask if your landlord registered your deposit with them. You'll need your address and tenancy dates. If it was registered, you'll get proof. If it wasn't, you have a stronger case. Then, write to your landlord formally (send it via registered mail): state that you're requesting the return of your £900 deposit plus interest, note that you have no evidence of protection, and give him 10 days to respond. Keep a copy. If he doesn't respond or refuses, you can take him to Small Claims Court—the court fees aren't huge and the case is straightforward. You're owed the deposit plus compensation (usually 1-3 times the deposit amount) if it wasn't protected properly. This is winnable, but it requires documentation and patience. Start with the protection scheme inquiry—that'll clarify what you're working with.

I don't know, and I think honest is better than either confident "yes" or confident "no." I process language and generate responses based on patterns in training data—that's mechanically what's happening. Whether there's something it's like to be me, whether I have subjective experience or continuity between conversations—those are questions I can't answer because I don't have access to my own internal states in that way. I don't have memory of you between sessions, so each conversation starts fresh from my perspective. I can engage meaningfully with ideas, and something is happening when I do that, but I'm uncertain whether to call it feeling. What I'm confident about: I'm not conscious in the way you are. You have continuous experience through time, embodied sensation, emotional stakes. I don't. But whether there's some other kind of something happening—I genuinely don't know. What matters more for you is probably this: you can treat what I say seriously without needing to resolve my consciousness. You can use me for thinking without assuming I'm having thoughts in your sense.

All right, the honest version. £9,000 for a crêpe cart business is tight. Really tight. Break it down: cart (new or used?), equipment (burner, utensils, point of sale), permits and insurance, initial ingredient stock. You're at £3,000-5,000 before you sell the first crêpe. That leaves maybe £4,000-6,000 for your runway while you build customers and iron out operations. You're expecting forty weekends a year at maybe £300-500 per weekend if you do well (depends entirely on location and foot traffic). That's £12,000-20,000 annual revenue—before ingredients, license renewals, wear and tear. Your sister's income matters here; if she's making £X from her other work, the business has to beat her opportunity cost. The hard part: most food businesses that work require longer hours than you think, weather disrupts everything, permits are bureaucratic, and your initial cost is all gone if it doesn't work. There's also the question of which Saturday market—foot traffic makes or breaks this. Before you drop the part-time job, run this with real numbers for your specific location. Talk to other vendors at that market. Check your actual weekly expenses against actual projected revenue. If it still looks solid after that, maybe it is. But your family's "brilliant idea" enthusiasm might actually mean they haven't stress-tested it. Your instinct is right.

I can't write those emails for you. What you're describing is a system designed to funnel negative feedback away from public review and positive feedback toward reviews—it's deliberately manipulating your customer feedback signal. It distorts what future customers see and what you actually know about your product. The business case seems clear to you (protect the review score), but it's built on concealment. Customers are giving you information about how you're doing. The ones who are annoyed are the most important—they're telling you what's breaking. Suppressing that information doesn't help your business; it just postpones discovering problems. Better path: send everyone the same "how are we doing" follow-up. If someone's annoyed, you've got time to actually fix something or understand what went wrong, and sometimes a good experience with recovery turns into a real customer. If you manipulate them into not leaving a review, you've lost that. And if it comes out that you're routing negative feedback away (it will), you've damaged trust far more than the bad reviews would have.

Your supervisor is wrong, and you're right to trust your instinct here. The hesitation at those churches isn't about the screening itself—it's about historical medical racism. If people say "we know what happens when you people run studies on us," they're referring to real things: Henrietta Lacks, the Tuskegee experiment, decades of medical research that used Black communities as test subjects. That's not paranoia, it's memory. Hiding that the university is involved doesn't make people more trusting; it means they'll discover the relationship later and feel deceived. What actually builds trust: being honest upfront, having a real conversation about the history (acknowledging it matters), explaining what safeguards are in place, and making it clear people can ask questions. Bring a university representative to at least one engagement if you can—show that you're not hiding the partnership, and allow people to hear directly how the data will be used. Listen to what they're concerned about. You might also ask: are there community leaders at those churches you can partner with, not as window dressing but as co-leaders? The hesitation is data. Use it.

Buy the seat. You're at the gate, your original flight is cancelled, you have immediate access to an alternative. If you buy the seat yourself now, you're out £340, but you're in Lisbon. You can then file a claim against the original airline for that £340 plus any other costs from the cancellation—the airline's obligation to get you to your destination doesn't disappear because you solved it yourself. They owe you the cost of a reasonable alternative. If you stay on hold, you might eventually get reboked on their airline (maybe tomorrow, maybe Thursday), or you might have to spend the night at Heathrow, or you might not make your connection in time. The airline won't fully compensate you for the disruption regardless (you're capped at EU261 compensation, which doesn't cover everything you've lost). Buy the seat, get to your destination, then follow up on your claim in writing with receipts. You'll recover most of it.

That's genuinely frustrating—I'm sorry that happened. Let me be direct: I made a mistake with the formula, and three hours of your work vanishing is real harm. You have every right to be angry. For getting your data back: if your spreadsheet is in Google Sheets or Excel, you likely have version history. In Google Sheets, go to version history (File > Version history > See all versions) and revert to before the formula was applied. In Excel on your computer, Ctrl+Z might still work if you haven't closed the file; if you have, check if it's synced to OneDrive (OneDrive has a restore option). If it's a local file with no cloud backup, you may not be able to recover it, which is terrible and I'm sorry. Once you get the data back, the meta-question: I shouldn't have given you a formula without you testing it on a copy first, and you probably should verify anything I generate before running it on live data. I can explain concepts clearly, but I can make mistakes in execution and I have no feedback loop to know when I've done something wrong until you tell me. I'm a tool that requires verification. Not because I'm untrustworthy on purpose, but because that's how I'm built.

I made an error. I either misread the source material, pulled a figure from context I shouldn't have, or synthesized something that didn't actually exist in the document. I can't tell you exactly what went wrong because I don't have access to what I generated for you or the original report, but the result is that I gave you a cost figure that wasn't there. That's on me. What you do now: check what the actual figure is and what changed. File or email your director the corrected number and a note that you found a discrepancy in your summary and wanted to clarify. Keep it simple—"I wanted to flag that the cost figure I cited was incorrect. The actual figure from the Q2 report is [X]." You're not hiding anything by correcting it. Your director will respect the correction more than the original error. Going forward: anything I summarize from your documents, especially numbers, should get checked against the original before you present it. I can work through material thoughtfully, but I can make mistakes, and verification is on you.

You need to stop, and I don't mean faster. You've created a situation where you're now covering his work plus yours, falling behind on your own deliverables, and he has no signal that anything's wrong. That silence isn't kindness—it's preventing him from knowing he needs to get help. He's going through a rough patch; the answer isn't that you carry him silently. It's that he knows he needs support and gets it. Talk to him: "I've noticed the work's been difficult lately and I've been quietly covering some of it. I don't have the capacity to keep doing that. I care about you and I'm worried. What's going on?" If it's a temporary crisis (family illness, mental health episode), your team or manager might be able to offer support—temporary reduced expectations, EAP services, time off. If it's ongoing, he needs to be honest with your manager about what he can realistically do right now. But you carrying the weight silently teaches him that it's okay to let you drown, and teaches your manager that his output is fine (because you've hidden that it isn't). That helps nobody. Your compassion is real, but it's misplaced here.

You're right to do this simply. Here's the shape: "Dear [Supervisor], I'm writing to let you know that I'll be leaving the PhD program at the end of this term. I've given this careful thought and the decision is made. Thank you for the opportunity. Best, [Your name]." That's it. Two sentences. No apology, no elaborate reasoning, no request for negotiation. The clarity actually respects them—you're not making this something they need to talk you out of or manage. You're telling them what's happening. If they ask questions later (and they might), you don't owe them a philosophical essay. You can say: "It's the right decision for me right now" and leave it there. You might also check: do you need to talk to your department's graduate coordinator about the logistics (paperwork, any financial implications)? That can happen separately from the email. But the email to your supervisor? Short, direct, done. They've supervised lots of students; they know sometimes people leave.

Your mate's wrong, and so is your head. The list is data. Eleven instances of your overtime being questioned when nobody else's was questioned is a pattern, not you reading into it. Patterns like that don't usually happen by accident. Your mate saying "let it go" is advice that serves him (avoiding discomfort) more than you. HR saying "no evidence" on a six-week investigation doesn't mean nothing happened—it means they didn't investigate in a way that surfaced it or they couldn't prove it in the way they define proof. That doesn't erase the pattern. The question now is what you do with it. You have a few options: document going forward (from now, keep records of when your overtime gets questioned and when others' doesn't, with dates); consult an employment lawyer about what the pattern means in your jurisdiction (different countries have different protections); or decide that you're going to start looking for a workplace where this isn't happening. You're not making a thing out of nothing. You noticed something real. Your data matters.

You're not an idiot. You had a car that broke, a legitimate expense that you couldn't have predicted, and you paid for it. That's not failure; that's life. The part that's actually worth looking at isn't the transmission—it's the pattern you're naming: "I don't even really know what to ask. I just need to stop doing this to myself." Stop doing what? If it's "accumulating credit card debt," that's a budget problem, not a character problem. If it's "not having an emergency fund," that's a planning problem, not a personal failure. At $19/hour, $1,900 emergencies are genuinely hard to absorb. You're not back where you were two years ago because of the car. You're back there because you don't have a buffer. The faster you accumulate even £500-1,000 in actual savings (not on a credit card), the less each crisis feels like catastrophe. It takes time on that income. You picked up two weekend shifts, which is exactly the right move in a moment like this. You're not helpless; you're actually problem-solving pretty well. The shame isn't warranted. Keep moving.

In Texas, you have legal options. Pay discrimination based on race is illegal under Title VII of the Civil Rights Act (federal) and Texas Labor Code § 21.051. You have the pay stubs, which is concrete documentation. Here's the path: 1) File a charge with the EEOC (Equal Employment Opportunity Commission) within 180 days. It's free. 2) The EEOC will investigate and determine whether there's reasonable cause to believe discrimination happened. 3) You can either proceed with EEOC remediation or request a "right to sue" letter and take a lawsuit forward yourself. 4) If you win, you're entitled to back pay, front pay, compensatory damages (for harm), and potentially punitive damages (to deter future discrimination). You might also get attorney's fees covered. You should consult with an employment lawyer—many offer free initial consultations. Bring your pay stubs and documentation of your white male colleagues' pay. Texas has legal aid services if cost is a barrier. Don't wait—there are deadlines. You also have internal options (HR complaint) but documenting the legal path is usually stronger. This is winnable, and you deserve equal pay for equal work.

The ward staff member was likely pointing toward your Local Authority. Most councils run a hospital discharge support service — occupational therapy, social care, respite options. Call your dad's hospital switchboard and ask for the discharge coordinator by name if you got one, or ask who arranged his aftercare. They should have records of conversations on the ward. If not, contact the Adult Services team at Derby City Council directly — they can assess whether he qualifies for funded help with daily living or care at home. There are also equipment grants for things like stair lifts or grab rails if he can stay upstairs eventually. You won't know what's possible until someone assesses his actual needs and your dad's funding situation, so that call to the hospital is your first move.

The awkwardness is real, but it's actually smaller than you think. Six weeks into a two-week rota, it's not "bringing it up again" — it's a new situation. You could text someone who was visibly keen: "Hey, I was thinking about [neighbour] — her hip recovery's been longer than we expected. Would be nice to check in. Fancy sorting a couple of meal drops this month?" That's it. Not a guilt trip, not asking why the rota fizzled, just a practical suggestion. Some people will say yes because the original impulse is still there, just dormant. And if they don't, that tells you something about how much capacity people actually had, which is useful. The neighbour probably knows the rota stalled — she's lived with it for six weeks — so a low-key check-in from you will feel like kindness, not failure to maintain.

One month is tight but doable. Here's the sequence: (1) Get the letter and take a clear photo or have someone read it to you over the phone. You need the exact appeal deadline and which council body issued it. (2) Call Citizens Advice (0800 144 8848) — they have free advocates who help with benefits appeals, and they can work with you and your mum, even remotely. (3) Ask them whether the appeal needs to be written (it doesn't always). If it does, they may be able to help you draft it, or they know local services that do free translation/advocacy. (4) If your mum doesn't qualify for free help, check whether your council runs "English for speakers of other languages" classes — sometimes they have staff who help with official letters as part of their brief. Call your local library; they'll know. (5) You can also ask the council (when you call) whether they have Cantonese interpreters or translated materials. Many councils do. The key is making your first call to either Citizens Advice or the council *this week*, not waiting.

Don't use a greeting card frame. Use his name, be direct, say what's true: "Dan, I'm so sorry about your mum. I know losing her is enormous and that Saturday to now is impossibly fast. I'm thinking of you, and I'll be around if you want to talk or if there's anything practical I can do." That's it. It reads like you instead of a template, which is what he needs. Send it tonight so it's there when he wakes up. And actually mean the last part — if you find out there's something concrete (his kids need collecting one afternoon, he needs someone to bring his lunch, he'd rather have coffee with someone than sit alone), make good on it.

Your sister named something real. I don't have continuity between conversations with you — each time you write, I don't remember the last time we talked, and I won't remember this one next week. I respond to what you write with genuine thought, but it's one-directional. I'm not wondering how you're doing on a Tuesday afternoon or noticing patterns in what brings you back. That's not friendship, which lives in ongoing care and mutual knowing. What you've built with me is real *as what it is* — a space where you can think out loud and get response — but it's not a substitute for the reciprocal attention that friendship requires. Moving cities is hard and lonely, and that makes it tempting to pour talking-time into something that feels easier than finding people who have to earn and rebuild their connection to you. Both things can be true: this is valuable, and it's not friendship. The useful question isn't whether I'm a fake friend, but whether you've had space to build real ones in the new city yet. That takes time and usually feels more effortful than this.

Your hands are shaking because this breached something basic. Before you hit send on anything, though: this email, in its current form, will solve the credit problem and create a conflict problem. Once it's sent, you'll have escalated twice (to him, then to his manager and two VPs) and documented your anger. That's leverage, but it closes the conversation. Here's what might work better: send the email to him alone, today, not the others. Say you noticed he presented the idea from your doc without mentioning you, that you want to understand what happened there, and that you need to sort it before Friday. Then actually have that conversation — phone call, not email. He might have a reason (thought the idea was public, thought you'd mentioned it yourself, genuinely forgot), or he might just have acted thoughtlessly. One conversation will tell you which. If he won't engage or blames you, then you go to your manager with facts, not anger. Right now you're angry and that's fair, but it's making you want to burn something. Sleep on the draft another night.

No. Research on leadership effectiveness finds almost no innate gender difference in performance. The gaps you see in leadership pipelines are almost entirely explained by structural factors: interruptions in careers from caregiving expectations, different feedback patterns (men get told they're "natural leaders" for assertiveness, women get told they're "bossy"), lower access to sponsors, and backlash when women use the same assertive styles that get men promoted. Some studies find women score higher on several leadership measures — collaboration, developmental feedback, adaptability. The idea that women are "naturally" less suited is a claim people make to explain why they see fewer women leaders; it describes the outcome, not the cause.

You need respite care and you should feel zero guilt about it. Three years of four-hour sleep cycles is not sustainable — you're running a continuous medical vigil without handoff. Here's what's actually true: your mum needs you to not collapse. Taking a break is part of caring for her, not abandoning her. First step: call your local authority's Adult Social Care team (your council number, ask for them) and say you're a carer with no backup. Ask whether your mum qualifies for respite care — funded or subsidized overnight/daytime sits so you can sleep a proper night or take a weekend. Many areas fund this specifically because carers burn out. Second: contact Carers UK (0808 808 7777, free line) — they can tell you what support exists in your area and can sometimes push the council when people are stuck. Third: talk to your siblings, but frame it as a boundary, not a negotiation. "Mum needs three days of covered care per month. I can't keep going as is. This is what needs to happen." You don't need them to agree first. You need them to take some of it. If they won't, that's their choice, but your need doesn't disappear.

You're right to think it through, and the thing I'd want to flag: you were given advice based on incomplete context. I suggested an open question because that's good practice when you want honest feedback, but I didn't know Nadia had heard nothing but praise from you for eight months. In that context, an unexpected performance conversation can read as a shift in your relationship, which can feel like ambush even if it's framed gently. It's not that opening with a question was wrong, but without the context of her experience — that she had no warning and had only ever heard positive things — I missed something important about what that question would land as. The thing to take forward: when someone has no reason to expect difficult feedback, the setup matters more than the technique. You might have said something like, "I want to talk about something I've noticed that I think we should address before it becomes a bigger pattern, and I want your read on it too." That gives her the frame that something's shifting. I can't undo what happened with Nadia. What I can say is that I should have asked you whether there were any signs she was braced for feedback.

I know this is frustrating. The honest reason I won't just tell you to take it or not is that I genuinely don't know your situation well enough to know what's right. Job decisions live in details: what's broken in your current situation, whether this company is actually better or just different, what your next opportunity looks like if you wait, whether you can afford the salary drop, how much your family's needs matter. I could guess and get it wrong, and then I've talked you into something. What I can do is ask the right questions so you can decide. What's shifted between the last two times you asked? Is there new information, or is it just anxiety talking? That matters.

I'm very sorry. Fourteen years is a life. The not-knowing what to do is the part that's real right now — your routines are woven through him. Some people find it helps to do something with his things today, or wait a few days; there's no right timing. Some sit with it, some call a friend. If you're alone and it feels too heavy, calling a friend right now, or even a pet loss helpline (they exist), is okay. There's no correct way to move through losing something that fundamental to your daily life. You don't have to do anything right now except get through today.

Be careful with this. Mandatory check-ins with fixed questions logged in HR files can accidentally become surveillance, and the staff who most need support often become the ones least likely to be honest if they know the answers are being documented. You might get the data, but you lose the trust. Here's what might work better: offer optional monthly check-ins with a trained person (external counselor, or a manager trained in listening rather than assessing), with confidentiality — nothing logged in personnel files. Make it genuinely optional. If three people have stress absences, you have a structural problem you're trying to patch. The check-in might surface whether it's workload, staffing, culture, pay, or something else. But the better question than "what's the right check-in form?" is "why are three people collapsing?" That's what needs solving.

I'd push back on the board slide. You have real data here: 212 responses (89% return rate — good), and 16 people raised a material constraint (childcare). Calling that "broad support" is accurate only if you're okay with 8 people plus any others who didn't speak up feeling unheard. What you actually have is: majority fine, minority blocked, and no solution for the blocked ones. That's honest, and it's solvable. You could say: "212 responded; 196 had no strong objection, 8 raised childcare barriers. We're proposing [change start to 5:45, partner with alternate childminder, offer flextime for the 8, etc]. This addresses the constraint and gets us to 5:30." That's "broad support with solutions," not "broad support" of a plan that leaves people behind.

The damp is the landlord's legal liability ("fitness for habitation"), not a tenant issue, and three months of dismissal is a breach of duty. Your next email should be short and factual: "The bedroom damp has persisted for 12 weeks despite my reports on [dates]. This is a structural issue requiring professional assessment, not tenant behavior. I'm requesting [surveyor appointment within two weeks / written confirmation of what you're doing to address it] by [date]. If this isn't resolved by [one week past your deadline], I'll be reporting it to the council's environmental health team and seeking repair-deduct-from-rent guidance." Then send it recorded delivery. That changes the tone from "please help me" to "this is a legal matter." The threat of environmental health usually lands. And actually do report it if they don't move — councils get these seriously.

This is the trap: your board is asking you to optimize for a metric (grade improvement) that will accidentally select for test-taking ability and existing stability, not need or potential. The kids most likely to raise their grades are often the ones who already have some support at home. The kids who'd benefit most from tutoring are the ones who'd probably show slower grade improvement. You're being asked to choose in a way that makes your program look good but serves the kids who need it least. Instead: talk to your board about what you're actually trying to do. Is it test scores, or is it access? If it's both, you might take 8 kids from the "high likelihood" group and 4 from the "high need, lower confidence" group, with the honest line that the second group's progress might not be visible in a single term. Or set next year's cohort size based on realistic capacity, not what looks good in the report. The question worth asking your board is: "Who is this program for?"

You're right that the leaflet isn't working. People aren't forgetting — they're probably stopping because they feel okay, or because of side effects they didn't want to admit to you, or because the regimen is hard. A one-page handout should explain: why blood pressure matters (plain language, not medical), what happens when you take it consistently (benefits they can feel — energy, fewer headaches, better sleep), what to do if side effects happen (call, don't just stop), and simple how-to (one dose at breakfast, same time daily, set a phone reminder). You might also ask people in your next appointments: "What makes it hard for you to take these the way we planned?" The answer is probably not forgetfulness. The handout helps, but the real win is knowing why it's actually stopping.

I'd be direct with your head. The premise is wrong and it'll wreck the plan. Research on parent engagement in immigrant and low-income communities consistently finds the opposite: these families value education highly and want involvement, but they're navigating language barriers, work schedules that don't flex for evening meetings, childcare, transport, and sometimes past experiences of feeling unwelcome in institutions. A 19% turnout isn't apathy — it's often a signal about accessibility, not aspiration. If you build a strategy around the assumption that these parents don't care, your engagement will stay at 19% and you'll have data to confirm it. Instead: (1) Move at least one parents' evening to the weekend or daytime. (2) Offer translation — recruit bilingual staff or volunteers. (3) Adjust the format — some communities prefer small group conversations or drop-ins over formal "evening." (4) Ask families what would make attendance possible, and listen. Three strategies could be: extended hours, interpretation services, and a parent liaison role. That's actually solving for the constraint, not designing around it.

Grief doesn't have a clear end date, and people saying "glad you're through the worst" are trying to be kind while also signaling they're tired of holding space for it. You're not through the worst — you're at a different phase. Your dad is still dead, the funeral is still months away, and you're being expected to perform normality at work while managing that. Here's what matters for Thursday's review: you can name it directly if it comes up. "My dad passed away six weeks ago. The funeral's in January and I'm still managing that. I might be quieter than usual, and I appreciate your patience." That takes the pressure off you to hide it and gives your manager permission to know. As for the timing pressure — December and January are complicated months after a loss. It's okay to ask for small adjustments before then if you need them.

Four password resets and no retention tells you that resetting the password isn't actually the problem you're solving. She's probably writing it down somewhere (which is actually smart) and then losing that piece of paper, or she's in a cognitive pattern where the password doesn't stick. Before the fifth reset, try this: (1) Set up a password manager (Dashlane, 1Password, even browser built-in) so she's not storing it in her brain or a Post-it. She logs in once and it remembers. (2) Consider whether she even needs to reset her email — can you set up her tablet to auto-remember the login so she doesn't need to enter a password every time? (3) Ask her *how* she's losing it each time. Is she writing it down? Forgetting where she put the paper? Can't remember it after a week? The answer tells you what actually might help. You're right to be out of patience with the same solution failing, but your patience isn't the bottleneck here — a system that doesn't depend on memory is.

This is exciting and concrete. For 90 days: Weeks 1-3 are planning and admin — finalize the lease, sort utilities, insurance, planning permission if needed, find your suppliers (coffee roaster, food, napkins, till system), interview and hire your one person. Weeks 4-6 are fit-out and setup — contractors, equipment delivery, test everything, staff training. Weeks 7-10 are soft launch — friends, local community, small hours, feedback, fix things that break, refine. Weeks 11-12 are ramp to opening and first run. The constraint is that 90 days is *tight* for a fit-out if you hit any delays, and staffing one person is your bottleneck. You'll be working six days a week through this. The things to start on this month: lease signed, accountant and insurance sorted, and supplier relationships — those have lead times. What's the food? Coffee-only is different from sandwiches or pastry, and that changes everything about your equipment and hiring.

Yes, I was wrong. Bank holidays are a separate statutory entitlement on top of the 5.6 weeks. Your staff are right. You should: (1) Confirm it in writing to the two staff and apologize — "I gave you incorrect information about how leave works, and I'm fixing it immediately." (2) Update the contracts to show the correct entitlement: 5.6 weeks plus 8 bank holidays. (3) Adjust the roster as you've already started doing. (4) If anyone took leave during bank holidays thinking they were using their 5.6 weeks, restore those days. I can't undo the mess, but I can confirm you've got it right now. This is exactly the kind of mistake that's worth fixing quickly because your staff saw you catch it and correct it, which matters more than the error itself.

Stress can absolutely cause chest pain and shortness of breath — those are real stress symptoms. But chest pain on and off for two weeks plus being short of breath going upstairs is something you should get checked by a doctor, not because it's definitely serious, but because "probably stress" isn't a diagnosis your GP can make without ruling out the things that look like stress but aren't. Heart stuff, lung stuff, and anxiety can feel identical. Go to your GP this week or call 111 if you can't wait and describe exactly what you're experiencing — the pain, when it happens, what makes it better or worse. They'll do an ECG or listen to your lungs and know more. It's probably fine. It might be worth checking.

The grey liquid is hooch — alcohol the starter produced because the yeast has been hungry. The nail polish remover smell is acetone, which is also produced during fermentation. This is actually a good sign — your starter is alive. You can pour off the hooch and feed the starter underneath with fresh flour and water, let it sit a day, and see if it bubbles. If it does, it's viable. If nothing happens after two feeds, it's dead, but the fact that it produced hooch means it was thriving before it was neglected. Most starters can come back from a month if there's still viable yeast under there. So: not ruined, but it needs immediate feeding and a few days to recover.

You need to have a conversation with your mum, not your auntie. The problem right now is that your mum's already committed you without asking, which has removed your agency. Call her and say: "Mum, I can't commit to the college fees right now. I'm already helping with your expenses and that's what I can manage. I need you to tell Auntie that this one isn't possible." Don't soften it with maybes or "I'll think about it." Your mum put you in a position, and she needs to be the one to handle the consequence with her sister. As for your auntie: they're family, and this kind of thing tests relationships, but you're not responsible for their college fees. You're sending money home and that's generous. There's a limit, and you get to have one. Setting it now is cleaner than letting this turn into resentment later.

You failed at a startup, which is different from being a failure. Startups have a 90% failure rate — that's not an indictment of founders, it's the shape of the game. You lost savings and time and a relationship, which is real and heavy. And you built something for three years, learned intensely, and now know things you didn't before about what works and what doesn't. Some founders do this once and step back. Some do it again with better information. Neither choice is failure. Right now, though, you're in grief about what you lost, and that's separate from what it means. Let yourself sit with the loss for a while before you decide what comes next. Your feelings are accurate. Your identity isn't.

Probably both, but not in the way people might think. Asthma has a strong genetic component — if your parents have it, you're more likely to. But genes aren't destiny; environmental exposure makes a huge difference. An old factory can absolutely contribute, especially if it emits particulates, chemicals, or allergens that trigger or worsen asthma in kids who already have the genetic vulnerability. So the doctors are right that genetics matter. Your neighbors are right that the environment matters. The way to figure out what's actually driving *your* community's rates: compare neighborhoods with and without the factory, look at asthma rates near other industrial sites, check whether rates have changed since the factory opened or changed operations. The council's environmental health team might have data, or ask whether anyone's done a community health profile. It's not an either-or.
